newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU seeks action to boost Europe's space industry.
newsitem.headline: EU seeks action to boost Europe's space industry.

text.p: The European Commission, anxious that Europe should not fall "hopelessly" behind in markets worth hundreds of billions of dollars, called on Wednesday for increased EU coordination on space.
"Europe does not want to be left behind on these very promising markets," European Union Research Commissioner Edith Cresson told a news conference.
Saying Europe must act quickly to capitalise on space applications, such as satellite telecommunications, satellite navigation and earth observation, she said.
"The idea is to encourage Europe to play an active role in the world competition which is underway to develop and master new resources from space."

The booming information society opened up new prospects, Cresson told reporters, adding: "There is spectacular growth in applications markets, particularly in the area of telecommunications by satellite."
The Commission's stragegy paper was worked out by Cresson, Industry Commissioner Martin Bangemann and Transport Commissioner Neil Kinnock -- reflecting the key areas affected.
Europe must quickly get its act together and adopt a proper strategy "if it is not to be left hopelessly behind", a statement by the EU executive said.
Cresson did not spell out which countries she regarded as Europe's major rivals in space, but she said last month the U.S. administration had thrown all its weight behind helping its industry.

The EU called for effective coordination between the different European players in the sector; the EU, its 15 member states, the European Space Agency, national agencies as well as operating organisations and users.
Growth in the industry bottomed out after 1992 due to cuts in government funding but this trend was likely to be rapidly reversed.
The global satellite telecommunications market is forecast to be worth 220 to 300 billion European currency units ($272 to 371.5 billion) over the next 10 years, the Commission said.
It plans to present an action plan early next year proposing a coherent EU approach to regulation and satellite communications.
The equipment market in satellite navigation and positioning -- used in the transport and tourism sectors -- was forecast to grow to 25 billion Ecus in 2005 from only 477 million in 1995.
Earth observation from space -- which may be of interest for sectors such as telecommunications, building and public works, fishing and agriculture -- was estimated at 30 billion Ecus.

The EU executive, well aware of widespread reluctance among member states to boost spending, stressed it was not proposing additional funding. Instead, the measures would be based on existing EU budget funds.
The three commissioners said they had created a space coordination group of officials which would be responsible for contacts with industry, national agencies and the European Space Agency.
The Commission also proposed boosting the role of the Space Advisory Group set up in 1993.

It would establish "appropriate structures" for specific projects and align trade policy positions, especially concerning commercial space launch services, and the allocation of frequencies and orbits.
